KorTTY protects your sensitive data with industry-standard encryption and centralized key management. All connection passwords, SSH key passphrases, and credential storage use AES-256-GCM encryption derived from a master password that is created on first launch.
On first launch, you are prompted to create a master password (minimum 6 characters) that encrypts all stored secrets.
Enter a password (the field border turns green when length is sufficient, red when too short).
A strength indicator shows password quality; a warning appears for weak or common passwords, but you can confirm if needed.
The master password itself is hashed with PBKDF2 (310,000 iterations) and never stored in plain text. The salt and hash are stored in KTPH000.

On subsequent launches, KorTTY prompts you to enter the master password to unlock encrypted data. Turning off KTPH000Require master password on startupKTPH001 in KTPH002Settings KTPH004 SecurityKTPH003 hides this prompt, but stored passwords will not be accessible until you enter the master password manually.

The second Security option, KTPH002Disable master password prompt on startup (auto-login)KTPH003, also removes the prompt but keeps the vault fully usable: korTTY writes your master password to KTPH000 — KTPH004obfuscated only, not encryptedKTPH005, with owner-only file permissions — and unlocks automatically on every start. The obfuscation key is embedded in the application, so file permissions are the only real boundary; anyone who can read KTPH001 or a backup can decrypt all saved secrets. On a brand-new profile the option bootstraps a default master password with no dialog at all. korTTY asks for confirmation before enabling it, it is meant for throwaway/test environments, and an KTPH006enterprise policyKTPH007 that requires a master password disables it. Details: KTPH008Security settingsKTPH009.
If you lose the master password, encrypted data cannot be recovered. Delete KTPH000 and KTPH001, restart, set a new master password, and re-enter your passwords.
All sensitive data at rest is encrypted using KTPH000AES-256-GCMKTPH001:
KTPH000Salt LengthKTPH001: 32 bytes (random per master password setup)
Each encrypted value combines a random IV with the ciphertext, encoded as Base64 for storage.
Store centralized username/password credentials that can be reused across multiple connections.
KTPH000EnvironmentKTPH001 — Production, Development, Test, or Staging
KTPH002Server PatternKTPH003 (optional) — Glob pattern (e.g., KTPH000, KTPH001) for automatic credential matching to connections
When creating or editing a connection:
Select a stored credential from the KTPH000CredentialsKTPH001 dropdown.
Username and password are filled in automatically.

Select the path to your private SSH key file.
(Optional) Enter the passphrase — it will be encrypted and stored.
KTPH000Centralized ManagementKTPH001 — Manage all SSH keys in one place
KTPH000Encrypted PassphrasesKTPH001 — Key passphrases are stored encrypted with AES-256-GCM
KTPH001Key CopyingKTPH002 — Use KTPH003Copy to User DirectoryKTPH004 to copy keys to KTPH000; copied keys are included in encrypted backups and restored with owner-only permissions

Select the desired key from the KTPH000SSH KeysKTPH001 dropdown.
The key path and passphrase are filled in automatically.

Terminal and SFTP connections, including the SSH bootstrap used by Mosh, share a trust-on-first-use (TOFU) verifier keyed by normalized host name and port. On first use, korTTY displays the server key algorithm and OpenSSH SHA-256 fingerprint; verify it out of band before accepting. The confirmation defaults to KTPH000NoKTPH001. A previously trusted matching key is accepted silently, while a changed key is hard-blocked with the expected and offered fingerprints and is never retried automatically.

Interactive pins are written atomically to KTPH000; a companion lock coordinates simultaneous korTTY processes. This store is distinct from the JobScheduler's connection-ID-based host-key pins in KTPH001, which protect unattended SSH, SFTP, and Rsync execution.

For lab or throwaway hosts you can turn the first-use prompt off and have korTTY accept an unknown key silently. This is an KTPH000accept-newKTPH001 relaxation, not blind trust: a key that differs from one already pinned for that host is still hard-blocked, so a man-in-the-middle on a host you have connected to before is still caught. It is off by default and can be set at three scopes, in precedence order:

KTPH000Per connectionKTPH001 — the KTPH002Host key verificationKTPH003 control in the Connection Manager's connection editor and in Quick Connect, with three states: KTPH004Use defaultKTPH005 (inherit), KTPH006VerifyKTPH007 (force strict even if the group or global setting relaxed it), and KTPH008Don't verifyKTPH009.
KTPH000Per groupKTPH001 — right-click a group in the Connection Manager and toggle KTPH002Disable host key verificationKTPH003; it applies to every connection in the group that inherits.
KTPH000GloballyKTPH001 — KTPH002Settings → Terminal → Disable host key verification for all connectionsKTPH003, the base default for every connection that inherits at both levels above.
A jump server's own host key is never relaxed by any of these — the bastion is always verified strictly.
Manage GPG keys for backup encryption and connection/snippet export encryption.
KTPH000Menu:KTPH001 Management KTPH002 Manage GPG Keys
KTPH000Manual EntryKTPH001 — Click KTPH002AddKTPH003 to enter key ID and email manually.
KTPH000System ImportKTPH001 — Click KTPH002Import from GPGKTPH003 to import keys from your system's GPG keyring.
Select a key from the list.
Click KTPH000EditKTPH001 to modify details, or KTPH002DeleteKTPH003 to remove.
Select KTPH000GPG EncryptionKTPH001 as the encryption type.
Choose the GPG key to use for encryption.
GPG-encrypted backups and exports are stored as KTPH000 files and require your system's KTPH001 command and a usable public key for decryption.
The following sensitive and security-related data is stored in KTPH000; secret values are encrypted, while public verification material is not:
SSH key paths and encrypted passphrases
Connection passwords (inline) and key passphrases (if not using SSH key management)
Trusted public host keys for interactive Terminal, SFTP, and Mosh bootstrap connections
Scheduler sudo passwords and archive passwords; journal entries redact KorTTY-managed secrets
Master password hash (PBKDF2, 310,000 iterations) and salt
Remembered master password for the optional auto-login
Obfuscated only — not encrypted; owner-only file permissions
AI profile API keys, translation API keys, optional Hugging Face token

Selected terminal text sent to AI services can contain sensitive information such as credentials, hostnames, file paths, stack traces, or operational details. For sensitive data, prefer an integrated local GGUF model, or verify that you trust the remote endpoint before sending anything.
Use a strong, unique master password (at least 12 characters, mix of upper/lowercase, numbers, symbols).
Keep private key files protected with a passphrase.
Copy keys to KTPH000 for inclusion in encrypted backups; keys left in their original locations are only referenced and must be migrated separately.

Verify a first-use host-key fingerprint through a trusted channel before accepting it. Treat a changed-key warning as a possible server rebuild, DNS error, or man-in-the-middle attack and investigate instead of reconnecting repeatedly.

KTPH000Host-key PinningKTPH001: Host keys are pinned by default for unattended SSH/SFTP/Rsync jobs to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks. These connection-ID pins are intentionally separate from the normalized endpoint pins used by interactive Terminal/SFTP sessions.
KTPH001Sudo PasswordsKTPH002: Scheduler sudo passwords are encrypted and stored in KTPH000.
KTPH000Journal RedactionKTPH001: Job journal entries redact KorTTY-managed secrets before persistence (redacted mode is the default; full mode stores unredacted output).
Always encrypt backups using either password-protected ZIP or GPG encryption.
Store backup files in a secure location.
Test restore procedures periodically to ensure backups are usable.
API keys for AI endpoints are encrypted with your master password.
The optional Hugging Face token is encrypted with the master password and is used only for approved model search/download requests to the trusted Hugging Face host.

Each integrated KTPH000 binds only to KTPH001 on a random port and requires a generated local API key. Offline mode is mandatory; web UI, agent, UI MCP proxy, slot endpoint, and inherited server-option overrides are disabled.

GGUF downloads require an immutable repository revision and exact SHA-256 metadata. Runtime indexes require an Ed25519 signature, and every runtime ZIP is checked against its signed size and SHA-256 before safe extraction. Official application builds embed only the public runtime-channel trust root; a missing or invalid key fails closed before any update request, while the signing private key remains isolated in the human-dispatched promotion workflow.

Signed runtime withdrawals are durable and fail closed. A verified index adds withdrawn runtime and installation IDs to KTPH000, marks each installed package, clears a matching active pointer, stops its sidecars, removes it from healthy rollback history, and quarantines affected model bindings. The installer and process launcher both reject those packages, including after an interrupted update. Notification-only checks enforce a withdrawal without silently installing the offered replacement; KTPH001OffKTPH002 makes no index request and therefore learns no new withdrawal until an explicit or enabled check.

A newly activated runtime is not promoted to healthy history merely because its bounded KTPH000 check passed. It remains pending until the first real GGUF-backed authenticated API start succeeds; that start failing removes the candidate and restores/rebinds the newest healthy non-revoked package when one exists.

Model recommendations and automatic prompt-family detection can refresh from a separate Ed25519-signed HTTPS catalog. The last valid cache is re-verified before use, and a monotonic sequence rejects signed older replays or equal-sequence version collisions before an atomic high-water update. Without the independent catalog public key, korTTY trusts neither network nor cache data and falls back to the built-in bootstrap. Production catalog and runtime signing are restricted to their main-branch, reviewer-protected GitHub environments; application builds receive only the public trust roots.
AI profile configuration is stored locally; only your reviewed terminal selection or prompt is sent to the chosen service. Embedded inference stays on this computer.

Knowledge-store scanning follows a fixed text allowlist, validates content, refuses symbolic links, and presents a preview. Only bounded retrieved excerpts, not the complete knowledge store, enter the model prompt. Those excerpts stay local for integrated/loopback profiles but leave the computer when an explicitly assigned cloud profile handles the request; knowledge-store roles and persisted profile assignments are the user's disclosure authorization.
Remote Qdrant knowledge stores require HTTPS; plain HTTP is accepted only for loopback, and the optional API key remains vault-protected.
Internet access is disabled by default for AI profiles; enable only when needed.
Snippet AI actions never use internet access, even if the profile has it enabled.
The fixed snippet/workflow KTPH000DiagramKTPH001 request never receives knowledge-store excerpts, even when the profile has stores attached — the diagram prompt is built from the source alone.
Encrypted with AES-256-GCM and master password
Shared normalized host:port TOFU, first-use fingerprint confirmation (optionally relaxed to accept-new), silent exact match, hard block on change
Encrypted with AES-256-GCM and master password
Loopback-only random port, generated API key, offline/hardened server flags, request leases
Immutable revisions, SHA-256 verification, signed runtime index, durable revocation quarantine, rollback after failed health check or first real API start
Independent Ed25519 trust root, strict schema, monotonic anti-replay sequence, reverified atomic cache, protected human promotion, bootstrap fallback
Central allowlist, UTF-8/PDF content checks, no symlink traversal, reviewed preview
Fixed retrieval limits, stable source markers, explicitly untrusted wrapper, explicit profile-based local/cloud disclosure
Master password stored obfuscated in KTPH000 with owner-only permissions; off by default, confirmation required, blocked by a policy that requires a master password
AES-256 password-protected ZIP or GPG-encrypted (legacy ZIP-encrypted backups remain importable)
Sudo and archive passwords encrypted; journal redaction enabled by default
Host-key pinning required by default for unattended SSH/SFTP/Rsync jobs
To change your master password (which re-encrypts all stored secrets with a new derivation):
Enter the new master password twice.

Every master-password-protected secret is automatically re-encrypted with the new key: connection and jump-server passwords, SSH-key passphrases, stored credentials, AI-profile API keys and the global AI/translation/Hugging Face keys, RAG store secrets, and JobScheduler sudo/archive passwords. The change is staged — the new password only takes over once every store has migrated, so an error part-way through leaves the old password in effect. Individual secrets that cannot be migrated are left untouched, counted in the result message, and noted in the log; re-enter those manually.
All KorTTY data is stored under KTPH000. Key security-related files:
